item.meaning: The 24-hour spinning motion of Earth around its own axis from west to east, creating sequential day and night on opposite hemispheres.
A living organism whose seasonal behavioral cues (such as bird vocalization or leaf shedding) indicate upcoming weather or climate shifts.

item.definition: The optical illusion of the Sun moving from east to west across the sky, caused by Earth rotating on its axis in the opposite direction (west to east).

item.title: Gnomon Shadow Elevation Angles
item.description: Solar elevation angle determines shadow lengths: low Sun angles at early morning/late evening cast long shadows, whereas high overhead Sun at solar noon casts the shortest shadow.

item.title: Biological Monsoon Indicators
item.description: Vocalizations of the Koel (cuckoo) bird in Odisha correlate with atmospheric humidity shifts announcing approaching monsoon rains, signaling farmers to time crop seed sowing.

item.principle_name: Principle of Planetary Axial Rotation (Diurnal Motion)
item.statement: Earth rotates on its central axis from west to east at a rate of 15° longitude per hour (360° per 24 hours), causing sequential solar exposure, day-night cycles, and apparent east-to-west solar motion.

item.cause: Earth rotating on its axis from west to east every 24 hours.
item.effect: Exposes longitudes to sunlight in sequence, creating alternating day and night and causing the Sun to appear to rise in the east and set in the west.

item.relationship_nature: Inverse Relationship: When the Sun is low on the horizon (early morning/late evening), shadow length is longest; when the Sun reaches solar noon high overhead, shadow length is shortest.
Mathematical Relationship: Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, so 15° of longitude pass under solar illumination every 60 minutes (1° every 4 minutes).

item.setup: Tracking the shadow cast by a vertical pencil (gnomon) on paper outdoors from 9 AM to 4 PM.
item.observed_phenomenon: The shadow points west in the morning, shrinks to its shortest length at noon, and lengthens pointing east in the late afternoon.
item.scientific_explanation: Reflects Earth's west-to-east axial rotation changing the apparent solar elevation angle throughout the day.

procedure: 1. Place a world globe on a table in a dark room and point a stationary flashlight at it.
2. Identify India on the globe and observe which hemisphere receives direct light.
3. Rotate the globe slowly from west to east and observe how day and night alternate across longitudes.
item.inference: Earth's axial rotation exposes different longitudes to solar illumination in sequence, causing 24-hour day-night cycles.

item.practical_use: Monitoring seasonal bird songs (like the Koel in Odisha) helps farmers accurately time soil plowing and seed sowing ahead of annual monsoon rains.
